statement: As summarized in two narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand and come from studies the reviews did not appraise, using more than one drug is common among people who use illegal drugs, how common depends on who was asked and how use was defined, and it makes the long-term effects of any one drug hard to study in people. Studies define it as using several drugs over a period (lifetime, or the past 1 to 12 months) or on the same occasion, the second being hard to capture in surveys and mostly studied in smaller high-risk samples; the DSM-IV diagnosis of polysubstance dependence was dropped from DSM-5, and most population research records only how often each drug is used. Studies that group people by the drugs they use typically find a limited range (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis), a moderate range (adding amphetamine-type drugs) and an extended range (adding prescription drugs used non-medically and other illegal drugs). Limited-range use was reported by 18% of 12- to 17-year-olds (ever) and by 34% of teenagers before 16, in two samples; extended-range use by 2% of 12- to 17-year-olds and 13.5% of 18- to 29-year-olds in Australian national samples, two different age groups that the review calls panel designs; and up to 75% of people at underground raves used several drugs, on average five at the last rave. Classes with a wide range of use reported more psychological distress, anxiety and depression in cross-sectional studies; several imaging studies and studies of self-control and decision-making found no difference in performance from comparison groups, although the review's conclusion states cognitive deficits as clear; and the authors judged research on preventing and treating the use of several drugs underdeveloped (Connor et al., 2014). In the ecstasy research reviewed in 2006, the great majority of people who used it also used other drugs, most often alcohol, cannabis and stimulants: earlier studies found cannabis use in 90% to 100% of people who used ecstasy, and in one survey everyone new to ecstasy (1 to 9 pills in all) had smoked cannabis in the previous month, 32% on five or more occasions. Studies that compared people who use ecstasy with people who use no drugs therefore cannot separate ecstasy from the other drugs; in studies with comparison groups who used other drugs but not ecstasy (up to 234 people who used ecstasy), raised psychological problems went with drug use in general rather than with ecstasy, though those comparison groups mostly used drugs more moderately; earlier studies often did not record other drugs; and findings on whether cannabis explains, adds to or offsets problems seen in people who use ecstasy pointed in different directions. The reviewers propose following young people at risk from before they start using drugs, for years, with drug histories recorded and psychological and cognitive tests repeated (Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann, 2006). How often people who use cocaine also drink or use cannabis, and what that means for cocaine research, is in the answer on cocaine with alcohol and cannabis. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: How common is using several drugs, and why does it matter? It is common among people who use illegal drugs, according to two reviews whose figures are second-hand. In Australian surveys, 2 in 100 teenagers and about 13 in 100 young adults used a wide range of drugs; at underground raves, up to 75 in 100 people used several drugs, five on average at the last rave. In ecstasy studies, 90 to 100 in 100 people also used cannabis, and many also drank alcohol or used stimulants. This makes it hard to know what one drug does over time: studies of people who use ecstasy may be measuring several drugs at once, and older studies often did not record the other drugs. The cocaine page has the figures for cocaine with alcohol and cannabis.
population: People in the samples two narrative reviews describe: national and student surveys (Australia, the USA, Brazil and elsewhere, mostly 2013), people at raves and clubs, treatment samples, and people who used ecstasy in the studies reviewed in 2006
exposure: Using more than one drug, over a period or on the same occasion, as each source defined it
comparator: None for the proportions; for research on ecstasy, comparison groups who used no drugs, or other drugs but not ecstasy
outcome: How common using several drugs is, and its patterns; whether studies of one drug can separate its effects from those of the other drugs used
magnitude: As described, not pooled, no intervals. Connor et al. (2014): limited-range use 18% of 12–17-year-olds (lifetime) and 34% of teenagers before 16; extended-range use 2% at 12–17 and 13.5% at 18–29 (Australian national samples of different age groups; 13.2% in the review's annotation of one source); up to 75% of people at underground raves using several drugs, on average five at the last rave; a sedative-and-alcohol class with last-year prevalence 1.3% among young Australian adults. Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann (2006): cannabis use in 90–100% of people who used ecstasy in earlier studies; in one survey all people new to ecstasy (1–9 pills) had smoked cannabis in the previous month, 32% on five or more occasions; comparison studies with up to 234 people who used ecstasy.

evidence.extracted: Polysubstance use is defined broadly as using more than one drug over a defined period, at the same time or at different times, for therapeutic or recreational purposes; in prevention and treatment it usually means several illicit drugs but can include licit and prescription drugs used non-medically.

risk_of_bias.note: Both sources are narrative reviews without search or appraisal (cards sc_connor_2014 and sc_gouzoulis_mayfrank_2006: editors' checklist, high), each drawing partly on its authors' own studies; the primary studies cannot be appraised here (METHODS §6.3).

inconsistency.note: The figures differ widely by population (2% of 12- to 17-year-olds with extended-range use, up to 75% of people at underground raves using several drugs), as the claim states; in every sample of people who use illegal drugs that the reviews describe (people at raves, people who use ecstasy), using several drugs is common.

indirectness.note: All figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3), mostly from Australian and US samples around 2013 and from the ecstasy research reviewed in 2006.

imprecision.note: No intervals are given; the figures are presented as descriptions of the samples, not as population estimates.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim resting only on two narrative reviews: it starts low (the primary studies are surveys and cross-sectional samples), is rated down one level for risk of bias (not appraisable) and one for indirectness (second-hand): very low; it stays at draft and out of the at-a-glance box (METHODS §6.3). The two reviews come from different groups, in Queensland in 2014 and in Cologne in 2006, and describe different primary studies; those of people who use illegal drugs all show that using several drugs is common: status replicated, as a description of those samples, not of any population. The health and cognitive associations in the first review are cross-sectional and are reported, not rated; its 2% and 13.5% compare different age groups in different samples, not the same people over time (card reporting issue). The cocaine figures (Liu et al., 2018) belong to the cocaine answer and are neither repeated nor counted here.
